South can guarantee a stopper in spades and at the same time ensure developing a ninth trick by simply not playing dummy's ♠Q at trick one. No matter how the defensive spades are distributed, East and West will have no answer to this play.
Once South gets on lead he can develop another trick in diamonds if that suit is divided 3-3. South only needs 9 tricks, however, and should take them without surrendering the lead.

notes: After East wins the ♠A, and returns a spade, South's only possible loser is in the trump suit. South must avoid losing a trick to the ♥Q.
South has 2 ways to play the heart suit worth considering. He could cash the ♥A and ♥K hoping for the ♥Q to be doubleton or singleton.
Alternatively, South could cash the ♥A or ♥K (in case West has a singleton ♥Q), travel to the dummy, and finesse East for the ♥Q by leading North's hearts through East.

The correct play is to take the heart finesse after cashing either the ♥A or ♥K. A famous bridge saying, 8 ever, 9 never, can help you remember this play. When you have 8 cards between the two hands, missing just the Queen, finesse (as in this hand). When there are 9 cards between the 2 hands, play for the drop.

When holding a 9 card fit missing just the Queen (as in this heart suit) it is correct to cash the top honours hoping the Queen is either singleton or doubleton.

When East has 4 spades, it is necessary to cash dummy's ♠A first. West shows out marking the 4-0 break. A spade is now played through East. East may play his ♠J or ♠10 but he is still helpless. South can cross to dummy (it is important not to have cashed all of the hearts and clubs) and a finessing position remains over East's ♠J.
Notice that if the ♠K or ♠Q is played first East will always take a spade trick by splitting his honours when a spade is led towards South.
There is no winning play if West has 4 spades. West can simply cover whenever South leads the ♠9 or ♠8 towards dummy, thus maintaining a sure stopper.
Therefore, the correct play is to lead the ♠A from North on the first round of the suit, guarding against East having all 4 spades.

notes: West leads the ♠9 against South's 3NT contract. South will have to knock out the ♦A to make his contract. There is a danger that the defense will be able to take 4 spade tricks after winning the ♦A.

If South plays the ♠J from dummy and the suit is distributed as above, East will cover with the ♠Q, placing South in a dilemma. If South wins the ♠A, East may have the ♦A and be able to lead through South's ♠10. If South holds up the ♠A for 3 rounds, he will fail when West has the ♦A.

South can ensure his contract by playing the ♠3 from dummy at trick 1. East will play the ♠Q and South can comfortably win the ♠A. South now has a guaranteed second spade stopper with his ♠10 and dummy's ♠J. The spade suit will also provide South's ninth trick after the ♦A is knocked out.

notes: South has 9 top tricks available (3 spades, 3 hearts, 2 diamonds, and the ♣A). North's club suit is the only possible source of extra tricks.
If South handles the clubs properly, 3 extra tricks can be taken any time West has the ♣K, the ♣Q, or both honours.

After winning the ♥J lead South should employ a technique known as a double finesse in his play of the club suit. This play amounts to leading South's clubs towards North's holding and only playing the ♣A if West follows with an honour. If the first finesse loses South has plenty of hand entries to play clubs through West 2 more times if necessary.

On the given lie of the cards, South can also succeed by cashing the ♣A, dropping East's singleton ♣Q, and then forcing out West's ♣K. This would be a poor play as it would fail many times that the double finesse succeeds.

If West was dealt 5 spades and the ♣A, there is nothing South can do. The contract will always fail on that lie of the cards.

As only 4 club tricks are needed in total, South can afford to give up a trick to the ♣K. The correct line of play is to win the diamond lead and play clubs immediately. The correct way to play clubs on this deal is to cash the ♣A and concede a trick to the ♣K. The ♥K can be used later as an entry to the dummy's long clubs.

There are 2 dangers on this deal. First, if the opening lead is ducked, a spade shift would be unwelcome. The defense may be able to establish enough spade tricks to defeat the contract when they gain the lead with the ♣K.

Second, after winning the opening lead, crossing to dummy's ♥K to finesse in clubs would also be wrong. This would take away dummy's sole entry to the long clubs. Notice how East can defeat the contract by not covering dummy's clubs with the ♣K.

If South plays on clubs first he will make his contract if West has the ♣K, regardless of the position of the ♠K. If the club finesse wins, North's club holding is worth 4 tricks and South will have a discard for his spade loser. If East turns out to have the ♣K, the contract could not have been made.
South should draw trump and play clubs through West's hoped for ♣K. South must be careful not to block the club suit. He should start with the ♣Q or ♣J on the first round of that suit.

On the second round, South should play the other high honour from his hand. The lead will still be in the South hand to take a third club finesse. The ♣A will remain to take care of South's spade loser. It would have done West no good to play the ♣K at any time.

notes: West leads the ♥K and continues the suit. After ruffing the second heart lead, South's only possible loser is in spades. South must try to prevent the defense from scoring a trick with the ♠K. South should not play the ♠A. That plan would succeed only if one of the defenders held the singleton King of spades.

Instead, South should cross to dummy and play a spade towards the closed hand. If East follows low, South should play the ♠Q (or any other spade besides the ♠A), taking a finesse. When the finesse wins, South can return to the dummy and finesse again. If East still has another spade left the ♠A will take care of it.
As South needs two dummy entries, he must be careful how he plays the diamonds. If South plays the ♦2 to the ♦K, he will have blocked the suit and be unable to return to the dummy.
South can succeed by leading his ♦2 to dummy's ♦10 or ♦9 the first time, finesse spades, and subsequently overtake his ♦Q or ♦J with dummy's ♦K.
Alternatively, South could overtake his ♦Q or ♦J the first time and, after finessing in spades, lead the ♦2 to dummy's ♦10 or ♦9.

It would be a mistake for South to duck the opening spade lead. The defense would switch to clubs, setting up 2 tricks there and making South's position virtually hopeless.

After winning the ♠A South should draw trump immediately. Next he should attack diamonds. South needs the defenders' diamonds to divide 3-2 to have a chance. Even with this break, South must be careful.
If South cashes North's ♦A and ♦K, and then surrenders a diamond, North's long diamonds will be good, but South will have no way to reach the dummy.
The solution is for South to duck either the first or second round of diamonds from both hands. After regaining the lead South will have a diamond in his hand with which he can reach the dummy.

A diamond trick must be surrendered at the end, but the contract is secure.
Notice that an initial trump lead would put the defenders one step ahead in the race to exhaust North's trumps. West can hardly be blamed, however, for leading from his attractive club holding.

notes: After the defense takes the first 3 spade tricks, and returns a club, South needs the rest of the tricks. Only six tricks are available in top winners (4 hearts, the ♦A, and the ♣A). One of the advantages of a trump contract, however, is that extra tricks are available by ruffing.
By employing the cross-ruff technique, South can score 8 trump tricks to go with the ♦A and ♣A. In order to do this, South must not draw any trumps.

After the ♣A and ♦A are cashed, the next 8 tricks will consist of club ruffs by North and diamond ruffs by South. The only danger remaining is that East will overruff North's ♥3 or that West will overruff South's ♥2. To minimize this risk, South should take these two ruffs first. After that the defense is helpless as all of the remaining North and South hearts are high.
The defense would have done better to lead trumps after cashing their 3 spade tricks. Due to the poor splits in clubs and diamonds, the contract would fail.

By the time a spade trick is established the defenders will be in a position to cash at least 3 heart tricks. 3 heart tricks along with the ♠A and ♠K will defeat the contract.

South must, therefore, look towards clubs for his ninth trick. If South leads a club up to North's ♣K at trick 2, a club trick can be taken any time West has the ♣A. This is another form of the simple finesse.

It would be a mistake to cash all of dummy's diamonds before leading clubs. The lead would end up in the wrong hand to take the club finesse. South's only remaining hand entry would be in hearts. Once South's second heart stopper is gone, West can simply take his ♣A and cash out hearts and spades.

After winning the opening lead, South should attack diamonds by leading the ♦K. The defense may duck the first round, but South continues diamonds with the ♦2, knocking out the ♦A.

Dummy now has an established diamond winner and the ♣A as an entry to it. The defense will continue spades, but South can win, cross to the ♣A, and discard his spade loser on the diamond winner in dummy. South gives up tricks to the ♥A and ♥K, making his contract.
It would be a mistake to play trumps before diamonds. The defense would win, and persist in spades. South would now be unable to avoid the loss of a spade trick.

notes: West leads the ♠Q against 4♥. South must lose a trick to the ♥A and West has attacked South's weak suit, spades. There is a danger that the defense will be able to take 3 spade tricks.
The ♠A is marked in East's hand as West would not lead the ♠Q away from the ♠A at a suit contract.
West is very likely to have the ♠J to back up his lead of the ♠Q.
If North's ♠K is played at trick 1, East will win the ♠A and return a spade through South's ♠10. The ♠10 will be trapped and the contract will be defeated.

South does better by playing the ♠4 or ♠5 from dummy at trick 1. If West continues with the ♠J, North's ♠K covers and East wins the ♠A. South's ♠10 is high. If West continues a low spade at trick 2, South plays low from North which will guarantee a spade stopper with either the ♠10 or the ♠K depending on which spade East plays.

When South gains the lead, he should draw trump as quickly as possible. If the defense holds up the ♥A until North is void and then plays either clubs or diamonds, South must be careful to trump the third round of that suit so that he can continue drawing all of the outstanding trumps. If South has any spade losers left, they can be discarded later on dummy's remaining diamonds and clubs.

notes: West leads the ♣Q which South wins. South's only possible losers are in the diamond suit. Unfortunately, there are 4 possible losers in that suit.

If South immediately draws trump, the defense might be in a position to take 4 diamond tricks if that suit breaks 4-2. South should delay drawing trump and play on diamonds at trick 2 with the aim of ruffing South's fourth diamond in dummy.

The defense might try to counter by leading spades, but the contract may still succeed. If the defender with the long diamonds has only 2 spades, he will have no trumps to play after winning the third diamond lead.
If it turns out that diamonds were 3-3 all along, South's long diamond will be high. There will be no need to ruff it in the dummy.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 3NT. South appears to have 10 tricks (the ♠A, 2 heart tricks, the ♦A, and 6 club tricks). The only possible problem is that clubs are breaking badly.
South must win the opening lead. Ducking is wrong as a spade or diamond switch would not be welcome.
South will be in trouble if he cashes the ♣A and ♣K, and finds clubs breaking 4-1. South can surrender a club trick, but there will be no way back to dummy to enjoy the long clubs.

South can guard against a 4-1 club break by ducking a club at trick 2. South can win any return and has a club remaining in his hand to reach the dummy. The defenders' remaining clubs will fall under dummy's honours.

South doesn't mind losing a trick in clubs as he only needs 5 tricks in that suit. This is an example of what is known as a safety play. A safety play is a precaution taken to guard against an unfavorable break (such as the 4-1 club break in this hand).

review.hl: NCA NCK NCQ NC6 NC5 NC4
NCA NCK NCQ NC6 NC5 NC4 SC3 SC2

notes: West leads the ♣10 against 3NT. South should try to establish and run dummy's diamond suit. Since only 6 diamond tricks are required (the ♣A, ♣K, and ♥A will be declarer's other 3 tricks), South can afford to lose a trick to the ♦K.

The contract is certain as long as South wins the opening lead in his hand with the ♣A. If South carelessly wins the opening lead with either dummy's ♣K or his own ♣J, and the diamonds break 3-0, the defense will be able to hold up the ♦K and prevent declarer from enjoying the long diamonds. South will then have no hope of scoring enough tricks in the other suits.
Notice that if East has 3 diamonds, you cannot succeed by winning the ♣K and finessing in diamonds. East simply will not cover with his ♦K and the contract will thus be defeated.

review.hl: NDQ NDJ NDT ND9 ND8 ND7 ND6
NDQ NDJ NDT ND9 ND8 ND7 ND6

notes: West's spade lead goes to East's ♠A. East continues spades and West wins. West will clear the spade suit. South has to make 2 discards from the dummy. What should they be?

The general concept of pitching low cards to keep high cards is a good one. On this deal, however, dummy has a very important low card that must be kept. The ♥2 has no value on this deal and can be discarded. The ♦2 is too big a little card to throw away.

If the ♦2 is discarded from dummy and clubs are 4-0, South will be able to cash just 7 tricks without surrendering the lead. The defense will be in a position to cash enough spade tricks to defeat the contract.

It should not be too difficult to part with a club from dummy's fine suit. South does not need 7 club tricks, just 3. Those tricks along with a spade trick, the ♥A, and 4 diamond tricks are enough to make 3NT.

With dummy retaining the ♦2 the suit can be played for 4 tricks (dummy's ♦A and ♦K must be cashed first). Notice also that South could have succeeded by discarding the ♦A and ♦K from dummy on the spades. However, he can't afford to part with the precious ♦2.

review.hl: NCA NCK NCQ NCT NC9 NC8 NC7
NDA NDK ND2 SDQ SDJ SDT SD9

notes: West leads the ♣5 against 3NT. South is fortunate to have escaped a diamond opening lead. West's choice of a club gives South a second club trick. That, along with 2 tricks in spades, 2 in hearts, and the ♦A, brings South's total up to 7.

Dummy's spades may provide an extra trick or two barring a bad break. The contract can be ensured, however, without depending on spades. South should turn his attention to clubs where the ♣K is the only high club out.
On most deals, declarer would be thrilled to win the first trick with a singleton queen in dummy. On this deal, if South lets dummy's ♣Q hold, the contract will be in danger.
South requires 2 hand entries, 1 to knock out the ♣K and another to cash the long clubs. Unfortunately, there is only 1 outside entry, the ♦A.
South must overtake dummy's ♣Q at trick 1 with the ♣A. After the ♣K is dislodged, the ♦A is an entry to the long clubs. South ends up taking 4 club tricks and making the contract.

review.hl: NCQ SCA SCJ SCT SC9 SC8
ESQ ESJ EST ES9 ES8 WS7
NSA NSK NS4 NS3 NS2 SS6 SS5
NCQ SCA SCJ SCT SC9 SC8

notes: West leads the ♥4 against 3♦. South should play the ♥J at trick 1. Not only is East almost certain to hold the ♥A, even if West had that card he would not underlead it. It is quite possible, however, that West has the ♥Q.
East wins the ♥Q and cashes the ♥A. East switches to spades and South wins in dummy. There is no reason to put off drawing trump. West wins the ♦A and continues spades, dummy winning.

After drawing trump, South must avoid losing 2 club tricks. When South leads a club and West follows low, South has a decision to make. If West has the ♣A and East has the ♣Q, it is necessary to play the ♣K from dummy.

The above distribution is unlikely, however, given the bidding. The above East hand has only 11 high card points, generally not enough for an opening bid. West's hand is also inconsistent with the bidding. Holding 2 aces, a doubleton, and trump support, West would have supported hearts instead of passing.
The above lie of the cards is much more likely. East has a full 13 point opener and West has only 6 points. If South plays the ♣K, East will win the ♣A and West will still get a trick with the ♣Q.
Therefore, South should not play the ♣K on the first round. Since dummy's lower clubs are solid, playing any one of them will do. East wins the ♣A and South makes the contract.

review.hl: ND3 ND2 SDK SDQ SDJ SDT SD9 SD8 SD7
ND3 SDQ SDJ SDT SD9 SD8 SD7
NCK NCJ NCT NC9 NC8 SC3 SC2

notes: West leads the ♥10 against 4♠. South should play low from dummy at trick 1 as it would be very unusual for West to underlead the ♥A. However, West's ♥10 might be from an interior sequence headed by the ♥Q. If this is the case South will lose only 1 heart trick if he plays low from dummy.

Unfortunately, East is able to win the ♥Q and cash the ♥A. East exits safely in clubs, dummy winning. South should draw trump immediately, finessing East for the ♠K, by leading the ♠Q. East does not cover the ♠Q, and South is able to repeat the finesse and draw the last trump.

South must avoid the loss of 2 diamond tricks. When South leads a low diamond, West follows small. If East has the ♦A, South should play a small diamond from dummy (all the diamonds below the ♦K are equals), hoping that West has the ♦Q.

The above lie of the cards is impossible, however. The East hand has 13 high card points and East failed to open the bidding. West must have the ♦A. If South plays a low diamond from dummy, East may be able to win the ♦Q.
As West must have the ♦A, South should play the ♦K, not a low diamond from dummy. South loses just 1 diamond trick and makes the contract.

review.hl: NSQ NS6 NS5 SSA SSJ SST SS9 SS8 SS7
NS6 NS5 SSA SSJ SST SS9 SS8
NDK NDJ NDT ND9 ND8 SD3 SD2

notes: West cashes the ♣K, ♠K, ♠A, and ♣A before exiting with the ♣J for South to ruff. South should draw trump ending in dummy and lead a diamond. South can afford 1 diamond loser, but not 2. In order to make the contract, South must guess whether to play the ♦K or the ♦J.

If East has the ♦Q and West has the ♦A, it is necessary to play the ♦J. West will win the ♦A and South will make the contract. West has already shown up with 15 high card points, however. The ♦A would make 19 points, too much for a 1NT opening bid.
East must have the ♦A and, if West has the ♦Q, it will be fatal to play the ♦J. South must instead play the ♦K. When that holds the trick, South makes his contract.

review.hl: SHK SHQ SHJ SHT SH9 SH8
NHA NH3 NH2 SHK SHQ SHJ SHT SH9

notes: West's spade opening lead establishes 2 inescapable losers for South. There is nothing to be gained from ducking the first trick so South should win the ♠A in dummy.

South has no losers in hearts or diamonds. South must hold his club losers to 1 in order to make the contract. South must hope that East has the ♣A. If West has the ♣A, the defense will always prevail.

South may have to lead up to his club holding twice. There are only 2 entries to the dummy, the ♠A and the ♥A. West has just knocked out 1 of them and South must use this entry to make a club play. East ducks and South is allowed to win the trick.
South should draw trump ending with dummy's ♥A. A second club is played through East who cannot prevent South from holding his club losers to 1.

If South had drawn trump immediately after winning the ♠A he would not have sufficient entries to lead clubs twice toward the closed hand. When East ducks the first round of clubs, the contract is defeated since South must then play clubs out of his hand.
